text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **
Roman Emperor CLAUDIUS was born in 10 BC. He was proclaimed emperor in AD 41 after CALIGULA was murdered.

The French zoologist, JEAN BAPTISTE DE LAMARCK, who coined the terms vertebrate and invertebrate to describe animals with and without backbones, was born in 1774. He also proposed that plants and animals inherited physical characteristics aquired by their parents.
United States poet, lawyer and author, FRANCIS SCOTT KEY, who wrote the American national anthem "The Star Spangled Banner", was born in 1779.
Explorer Sir AUGUSTUS GREGORY, who opened up much of Queensland to pastoral settlement, was born in 1819.
American novelist HERMAN MELVILLE, who wrote "Moby Dick", was born in 1819. He was a cabin boy on a whaling ship, and once joined in a mutiny aboard an Australian ship.
Australian cattle pioneer WILLIAM BEIT, who ran a property near Toowoomba in Queensland called 'Westbrook', was born in 1829.
The first Australian knighted for services to medicine, Irish/Australian Sir THOMAS FITZGERALD, was born in 1838.
Australian actress PAT MCDONALD, who leapt to national recognition as "DORRIE EVANS" in "Number 96", was born in 1923.
British songwriter, LIONEL BART, was born in 1930. He wrote "Living Doll" for CLIFF RICHARD and "Do You Mind" for ANTHONY NEWLEY. He also wrote the script, music and lyrics for the musical "Oliver".

British singer/ songwriter with 'Def Leppard', JOE ELLIOT, was born in 1959. Hits include "Photograph" (1983), "Rock Of Ages" (1983), "Animal" (1987), "Hysteria" (1987), "Love Bites" (1988) and "Pour Sugar On Me" (1989).
** EVENTS **
1498 : CHRISTOPHER COLUMBUS landed on mainland America,
but thinking it was an island, called it Isla Santa.
1774 : British chemist Sir JOSEPH PRIESTLEY announced
that he had discovered oxygen.
1778 : The first savings bank opened in Hamburg in
Germany.
1793 : France became the first country to use the metric
system of weights and measures, a byproduct of the French Revolution. The length of the metre was based on a fraction of the earth's circumference that was calculated incorrectly.
1798 : British fleet under Lord NELSON defeated the
French fleet at the Battle of the Nile, thwarting Napoleon's conquest of the Middle East.
1831 : The new London bridge was opened by WILLIAM IV and
Queen ADELAIDE.
1834 : Slavery was abolished throughout the British
Empire; an estimated 770,280 slaves became free.
1840 : An Order in Council took effect, ending the

transportation of convicts to New South Wales. 111,500 convicts had been sent to the new (Australian) colony since 1788, and while New South Wales was the first to stop the importation, the rest of the nation took 10 years to follow suit.
1914 : As World War One approached, Germany declared war
on Russia, shots were fired between French and German border patrols and Italy declared her neutrality.
1921 : The first release of MAY GIBBS' "Snugglepot and
Cuddlepie" had sold 17,000 copies. GIBBS created authentic Australian images based on her observation of the bush.
1936 : ADOLF HITLER opened the 11th Olympic Games in
Berlin.
1939 : Band leader GLENN MILLER recorded the song "In the
Mood."
1944 : The 63-day Warsaw uprising began when Poles rose
against the Nazi occupation.
1950 : Australian Prime Minister Sir ROBERT MENZIES
promised to send troops to South Korea to join UN forces in repelling the invasion by North Korea.
1965 : The labor party deleted the words "White
Australia" from its immigration policy, calling the term inaccurate and offensive.
1979 : A report estimated that tax avoidance schemes had
deprived the Australian government of 420 million dollars in the 1978/79 financial year.
1983 : PAUL SHARP became the first white person to cross
Australia's Simpson Desert alone, and on foot.
1985 : The United States agreed to sanctions against
South Africa in protest against apartheid.
1986 : Swiss historian FRITZ MATHY WEIST exploded the
myth of national hero WILLIAM TELL's reported feat of shooting an apple from his son's head with a crossbow. WEIST pointed out that the crossbow was unknown in Switzerland in the 13th century.
1988 : Anglican Bishops in London voted in favour of the
ordination of women.
1989 : A group of 16 English cricketers announced they
would tour South Africa.
1994 : German President ROMAN HERZOG apologised for the
suffering his nation caused Poland in World War Two.
1995 : France recalled its ambassador to Australia after
the protests over French nuclear tests.
